title: Kafka ordering per partition
prompt: An order service publishes all events for one order to a Kafka topic with 6 partitions, using the order id as the record key. Which ordering guarantee holds?
options: Events for one order arrive in order; events across different orders may arrive in any order.
All events in the topic arrive in the order they were published.
Events for one order may arrive out of order, but each partition is ordered.
Ordering is only guaranteed if the consumer group has exactly one member.
answer: Events for one order arrive in order; events across different orders may arrive in any order.
explanation: Kafka orders within a partition, and the key hashes to one partition — so one order's events stay ordered. Across partitions (different orders) there is no global ordering.

title: Dead-letter topic for poison messages
prompt: A @KafkaListener throws on every attempt for one record. With a DefaultErrorHandler and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer configured, what happens after the retries are exhausted?
options: The consumer stops and the application must be restarted.
The record is published to a dead-letter topic and the consumer commits the offset and moves on.
The record is silently dropped and its offset is never committed.
The whole consumer group rebalances and the record is retried from the start.
answer: The record is published to a dead-letter topic and the consumer commits the offset and moves on.
explanation: After the configured retries with backoff, the recoverer publishes the failed record to the dead-letter topic (original topic plus -dlt) and the container commits the offset, so one poison message cannot block its partition.

title: condition vs unless on @Cacheable
prompt: A method is annotated @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id", condition = "#id > 0", unless = "#result == null"). Which statement is correct?
options: condition is checked after the method runs and can use #result; unless is checked before and can only use the arguments.
condition is checked before the method runs using only the arguments; unless is checked after and can use #result.
condition and unless are checked at the same time, before the method runs.
unless prevents the method from running when the result would be null.
answer: condition is checked before the method runs using only the arguments; unless is checked after and can use #result.
explanation: condition is evaluated before the call (arguments only), unless after the call (#result available). They are not interchangeable: only unless can judge the computed value.

title: @Cacheable sync=true
prompt: A hot cache key expires while 100 requests arrive at once. The method is annotated @Cacheable(value = "prices", key = "#id", sync = true). What happens?
options: All 100 requests hit the database at once; sync only works for @CachePut.
The first request loads the value and the other 99 wait on it, so the database is hit once for that key.
The 100 requests are spread across all caches named in the annotation.
Spring returns a stale value to 99 requests and loads fresh data for one.
answer: The first request loads the value and the other 99 wait on it, so the database is hit once for that key.
explanation: sync=true makes concurrent misses for the same key wait on the first loader, preventing a cache stampede. It works for a single cache only.

title: ProblemDetail media type and fields
prompt: A Spring Boot 3 application returns a ProblemDetail from an @ExceptionHandler for a missing user. Which response is correct?
options: Content-Type: application/json with a body of {"error": "User not found"}.
Content-Type: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance members.
Content-Type: text/html with the default Whitelabel error page.
Content-Type: application/problem+json with only a status member; the other members are optional.
answer: Content-Type: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance members.
explanation: ProblemDetail implements RFC 9457: the standard body has type, title, status, detail, and instance, served as application/problem+json. Returning it from a handler sets the status and content type from the object.

title: Shallow vs deep copy with clone()
prompt: A Team class implements Cloneable and overrides clone() with return (Team) super.clone(); only. Its members field is a mutable List<String>. What happens when the clone's list is modified?
options: The original's list is unchanged, because clone() always deep-copies mutable fields.
The original's list changes too, because super.clone() is a shallow copy and both objects share the same list.
CloneNotSupportedException is thrown, because the class does not deep-copy its fields.
The clone's list is empty, because super.clone() does not copy collection fields.
answer: The original's list changes too, because super.clone() is a shallow copy and both objects share the same list.
explanation: Object.clone() copies fields, not the objects they point to — a shallow copy. Without an explicit new ArrayList<>(members) the clone and the original share one list.

title: Suppressed exceptions
prompt: In a try-with-resources block, the try body throws IOException("work failed") and closing the resource throws IOException("close failed"). What does the catch block see?
options: Only "close failed": the close exception replaces the body exception.
Only "work failed": the close exception is lost.
The primary exception "work failed", with "close failed" attached as a suppressed exception retrievable with getSuppressed().
Both exceptions are chained with initCause, so getCause() returns "close failed".
answer: The primary exception "work failed", with "close failed" attached as a suppressed exception retrievable with getSuppressed().
explanation: Try-with-resources keeps the body's exception as primary and attaches the close exception with addSuppressed. If the body succeeds and only the close throws, the close exception becomes primary.

title: StructuredTaskScope API version trap
prompt: Code written for Java 21 uses new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure(), scope.join(), and scope.throwIfFailed(). What happens when it is compiled on JDK 25?
options: It compiles unchanged: the API is final since Java 21.
It fails to compile: JDK 25 (JEP 505) replaced the constructors with StructuredTaskScope.open() and a Joiner, and join() itself throws.
It compiles but throws at runtime, because preview APIs are removed in JDK 25.
It compiles with a deprecation warning only; ShutdownOnFailure still exists as an alias.
answer: It fails to compile: JDK 25 (JEP 505) replaced the constructors with StructuredTaskScope.open() and a Joiner, and join() itself throws.
explanation: Structured concurrency stayed in preview and JDK 25 reworked the API: open() factories with a Joiner policy, fork() returning Subtask instead of Future, and no throwIfFailed(). Java 21–24 code does not compile on JDK 25, and both need --enable-preview.

title: ScopedValue vs ThreadLocal
front: What is a ScopedValue, and why is it a better fit than ThreadLocal for virtual threads?
back: An immutable binding that exists only inside its scope (ScopedValue.where(...).run(...)) and is inherited by virtual threads forked inside it — it cannot leak between requests. A ThreadLocal is copied per virtual thread and can bleed into the next request if left uncleared. Preview in Java 21–24, final in JDK 25 (JEP 506).

title: @MethodSource provider rules
front: When do you use @MethodSource, and what must its provider method be?
back: Use @MethodSource when parameterized cases need objects or computation that does not fit in a @CsvSource string. The provider names a factory method returning a Stream (or Iterable/array) of Arguments — one per case — and it must be static unless the class uses @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS).

title: Exactly-once in Kafka
front: What does exactly-once mean in Kafka, and where does it stop?
back: Within Kafka: an idempotent producer plus transactions, read by read_committed consumers, gives effectively-once. Across Kafka and another system (a database, an HTTP call), Kafka alone cannot give it — use an idempotent consumer or the transactional outbox pattern.

title: Redis cache serialization in Boot 3.x
front: How should Spring Cache values be serialized to Redis in Spring Boot 3.x, and which serializer must you not copy from old tutorials?
back: Use GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer for values (JSON, survives class changes) and StringRedisSerializer for readable keys. Do not use Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer — it is deprecated in Spring Data Redis 3.x — and remember Boot 3.x connection properties live under spring.data.redis.*, not spring.redis.*.
